description: We’re building a web tool for NASA’s SPHEREx data. Type in sky coordinates and watch stars, brown dwarfs and asteroids move over time. Looking for: Python/data folks, frontend web devs, and designers/storytellers. No astronomy background needed, just curiosity and commitment!
summary:
Something out there is moving. Can you spot it?

Somewhere in NASA's infrared images, cold and elusive neighbours of our Sun are quietly wandering across the sky. The catch? They're really good at hiding.

Meet Wanderer, a free citizen-science app that turns NASA's latest SPHEREx all-sky images into a cosmic game of spot-the-difference. Blink between two images of the same 20′ patch of sky, taken months apart. Spot something that moved? Click it. No astronomy degree required; planted practice movers help you learn the ropes.

Behind the scenes, every candidate is cross-matched against Gaia DR3 and CatWISE, screened through six glitch-detection tests, and analysed using SPHEREx's 102-colour infrared spectra to distinguish cold brown dwarfs from dusty galaxies and ordinary stars.

Want to play detective beyond the blinking game? The Sky Explorer offers a 3D map of stars within 15 light-years, historical observations, difference images, spectra, and downloadable reports.

We've tested the pipeline on real data, recovering 88–100% of injected artificial movers (W2 ≲ 14, ≥ 12″/yr), with zero false alarms across 80 tests. GitHub Actions automatically adds fresh SPHEREx Quick Release 3 data every week, with zero running costs.

The next cold neighbour of the Sun might be hiding in plain sight. You might be the one who finds it.
details:
What does wanderer do?

Wanderer turns NASA SPHEREx images into a citizen-science search to spot objects that move or change over time. From nearby fast-moving stars and elusive cold brown dwarfs to asteroids and variable stars, Wanderer helps turn curious clicks into real astronomical discoveries.

How does it work?

A Python pipeline queries NASA IRSA for every SPHEREx DR1 and Quick Release 3 exposure covering a position, downloads cut-outs from all six detectors, groups them into epochs, and builds median stacks. Gaia DR3 and CatWISE stars are propagated to the SPHEREx date. In the browser, per-detector difference images in σ units reveal changes; “Find movers” pairs bright/faint dipoles (≥ 6σ) into candidates. Each candidate gets a VET score (0–100) from six artefact tests, with vetoes for bright-star glare and alignment errors, plus a spectral classification from water (1.4 µm) and methane (3.3 µm) absorption. Candidates can be logged, inspected, and exported as a full report (PDF/CSV).

Two interfaces

“Spot the Wanderer” (home page) is a Zooniverse-inspired classifier with a 5-step tutorial and planted practice movers; marks go anonymously (optional name for discovery credit) to a Google Sheets database via Apps Script. The Sky Explorer offers a 3D star map, Aladin Lite sky view, every epoch, blink/difference/colour/every-frame modes, and a red-source survey.

Does it actually work?

Injection–recovery: 88–100% of fake movers recovered (W2 ≲ 14, ≥ 12″/yr), 0/80 false movers. Field-star control: 49/49 classified as normal stars. Blind survey of 38 extremely red CatWISE sources: 0/30 non-moving sources mislabelled as brown dwarfs; 12/12 wide-field alignment artefacts caught. Testing exposed real bugs (a gate that discarded faint movers, a classifier that called galaxies brown dwarfs), which we fixed and re-tested. Internal playtest: 4 testers, 24 fields, 60% of practice movers found. Limits: objects fainter than W2 ≈ 15 and movers slower than ~6″/yr are not yet recovered.

Why does it matter?

NASA’s Backyard Worlds volunteers doubled the known brown dwarfs using WISE, which has now retired. SPHEREx is the new repeating all-sky infrared survey, and Wanderer is built to grow with it! Every new survey lengthens the baseline and brings slower, fainter movers into reach.

Tools used

Python (NumPy, Astropy, Astroquery, FastAPI), JavaScript, Three.js, Aladin Lite, Playwright, GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions, Google Apps Script. Code: https://github.com/kipasangin-kejepit/wanderer

Use of AI

Much of the code, brainstorming, translating, and gathering information (instead of using google) were written with the help of Claude by Anthropic, under our direction; the team chose the problem, the design and the scientific approach, tested and reviewed the results, and is responsible for the project.
